docs.title: Install and toolchain
docs.text:
Nothing acquires at all, or the acquisition binary cannot be found. The acquisition engine's build artifacts are missing. The submodule ships Windows binaries only; on Linux they must be built from the submodule's source.

SoapySDR.dll: cannot open shared object file. The acquisition engine's tracking binaries link it eagerly and will not start without it, even for file replay with no hardware. Its acquisition binary does not, so the measurement path is unaffected: it costs four determinism tests and the enrichment path, nothing else. See Installation.

The whole test suite skips. The acquisition engine's submodule is not on its pinned commit, and the suite skips rather than fails. A run that is all s is not a passing run. See Installation.

The test suite hangs, or pegs every core. Cap the BLAS thread count before numpy is imported. Uncapped on a 48-core box the suite spawns 128 threads and does not finish; capped it takes about three minutes. Setting the variable after numpy loads does nothing. The suite's own configuration handles this; your own scripts must do the same. Run correlator-scale jobs one or two at a time, with OMP_NUM_THREADS=8.

docs.title: Measuring
docs.text:
Everything says too_short. The capture is below the detectors' minimums. Run validate: it names each detector, its minimum and the reason, before you spend anything.

Results did not change after I edited something. Stage results are cached on inputs, arguments, acquisition engine commit and tool version. Pass --force.

correlate measured more signals than acquire found, or the report lists a satellite the capture no longer contains. The store predates 2026-08-25 and holds rows from an earlier run. gnss-vsa acquire --force <manifest> rewrites the census, and correlate follows it. Deleting the store also works, but costs a full re-correlation.

A satellite acquires with a plausible C/N0, and is not in the scenario. A cross-correlation peak at the acquisition threshold is a real acquisition of the wrong thing, and the 38 dB-Hz acquisition threshold is tuned for RF, not for a noiseless digital source. On one hot satellite with no noise, every searched PRN can clear it. Check the margin:

gnss-vsa query store "SELECT sat, cn0_dbhz, acquired FROM acquisitions ORDER BY cn0_dbhz DESC"

C/N0 is 80–95 dB-Hz and wanders, on a single-satellite noiseless capture. The estimator's denominator is numerical residue: there is no noise. It is not a measurement. Compare prompt amplitude instead.

The numbers are plausible, but wrong on every satellite. Suspect the format before the signal. A misread dtype or interleave produces plausible numbers, not an error. See Next to a DUT.

Every Doppler has the wrong sign. spectral_sense (or, equivalently, iq versus qi) is the wrong way round. It is one bit, carried by either field: flip one, not both.

docs.title: Interpreting
docs.text:
ripple fires at one cycle per sample of delay traversed. Before attributing it to the generator, run tools/probes/probe_replica_placement.py. That period is equally the signature of an instrument that cannot place its replica. It has happened.

ripple and step both fire on one series. Read the ripple row first. step responds to a slow periodic error and names it a step.

Inter-element differences are exactly zero, but each element shows structure. That structure is common mode, and differencing cancels it by design. Differences answer element-to-element consistency, not whether the generator is right.

An absolute delay on a long capture is off by a few centimetres, differently per satellite. refine assumes a constant Doppler, which leaves −aT²/12 at the start epoch. See Reading results honestly.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
Example cases: defects the VSA found in a generator under test, and errors it found in itself.

The GNSS VSA is a standalone tool for testing and analysing any GNSS simulator or signal generator. The cases below come from measuring a software GNSS simulator under development. They are not a review of that simulator. They show what kind of defect the tool can find, how it decides whose defect a result is, and what it costs when it gets that wrong.

Every case follows the same rule: the generator is a device under test, never a reference. A result counts only when it is checked against truth that the generator did not produce, such as an injected test signal, a bench at a delay the tool chose, or plain geometry.

  • A constant half-sample timing bias

    Every satellite arrived exactly half a sample early, whenever the sample rate was a whole multiple of the chip rate: 12.2 m at 12.276 MHz. No receiver would see it in a position fix. Three independent checks settled whose it was.

    Read the case

  • Code jumps at every power-of-two second

    Bursts of ~0.22 samples (5.4 m) of late code, starting at elapsed times of exactly 2^k seconds and doubling in length each time. One rounding decision at an exact chip boundary caused it.

    Read the case

  • The instrument's own errors

    The tool's first published finding turned out to be its own. That case, and four more the tool found in itself, are why every result is screened against the instrument before it is attributed to a device.

    Read the case

docs.title: What the cases have in common
docs.text:
• None would show in a receiver's position fix. A bias common to every satellite of a signal goes into the clock estimate. Short transients are smoothed by the tracking loops. The tool measures open-loop because those are the defects that hide.
  • Small structure needs one strong signal. With many satellites at equal power and no thermal noise, each satellite's noise floor is the others. Raising one satellite clear of the rest dropped the per-epoch scatter from 0.12 to 0.0024 samples, and that is what made the power-of-two jumps visible at all.
  • Attribution is a separate experiment from detection. Each case was detected by a detector or a residual, then attributed by tests whose possible explanations predicted different outcomes.
  • Fixes are verified by re-measuring, not by inspection. Each generator fix was accepted only after the same captures, at the same settings, read clean through the same instrument.

docs.title: The instrument's own errors
docs.text:
The tool's first published finding was about the tool. That case, and the ones that followed it, are why every result is screened against the instrument before it is attributed to a device.

A measuring instrument can manufacture exactly the structure it is built to detect. These are the cases where this one did. Each was found, fixed and then held by a test, and each changed how results are read.

docs.title: 1. The first finding was ours
docs.text:
What was seen. On the first multi-element capture, the measured code offset carried a periodic error whose period was exactly the time the commanded delay took to cross one sample, matching the Doppler prediction to within 1 % on every satellite, at 0.16–0.42 samples. A null test on a synthetic signal showed nothing, so it was published as the generator's interpolator ripple.

What it was. The correlator's replica placed chip edges by a truncated index, so it could not put an edge between samples. The fractional part of the code offset was silently discarded, and came back as a ±0.5-sample sawtooth at exactly that period. The null control missed it because the synthetic signal snapped its chip edges by the same rule: the fixture and the replica quantized together, and the error cancelled by construction. The control was sound for every failure except the one it was built to rule out.

What changed.

  • The replica now applies the fractional delay exactly, as a band-limited phase ramp.
  • The synthetic fixtures place chips by a deliberately different model (integrate and dump in time, rather than a phase ramp in frequency), so agreement is evidence rather than a tautology.
  • The original finding was retracted as to attribution, not deleted. The measurement and the period relation were right; whose error it was was wrong.
  • tools/probes/probe_replica_placement.py pins the pointer to the truth and sweeps a whole sample of delay. Every number it prints should be zero. Run it before attributing a ripple at this period to any device.

Re-run on the same capture, the ripple detector went from firing on 5 of 8 series to 0 of 32.

docs.title: 2. A navigation data bit broke two estimators
docs.text:
What was seen. On the same capture, some satellites showed single-epoch code excursions of tens of samples, and C/N0 read about 28 dB-Hz against a code scatter implying thirty times more signal.

What it was. A 50 bps navigation bit inverts the prompt correlation. The carrier fit unwrapped the plain phase angle and could not tell a half-cycle data step from a real one. It was wrong by 5–9 Hz at every C/N0, which is about 0.79 samples (19 m) of code offset. The C/N0 estimator's coherent mean cancelled on the same bit, and read about 17 dB-Hz whatever the true value.

What changed. The carrier is fitted on the doubled angle, which removes the ±1 modulation, and the bit is removed before power is estimated. On the capture, code error went from 10.4 to 0.08 samples on the worst satellite with no epochs rejected, and C/N0 read 50–54 dB-Hz. The cost is stated: below about 38 dB-Hz on a 1 ms epoch, the per-epoch bit decision gives out.

docs.title: 3. The discriminator's gain was assumed, not measured
docs.text:
What was seen. On Galileo E1B, refinement never settled: it overshot the null and kept oscillating around it.

What it was. The early-late balance was converted to samples with the slope of an ideal triangle. The real slope is steeper by 2.1× on E1B (its BOC correlation peak is narrow) and 1.2× on L1 C/A. A gain of 2 is exactly where a correction stops shrinking the error and just flips its sign. Every E1B pointer had been sitting about 0.6 samples (15 m) off the null.

What changed. Four probe taps around the early/late pair measure the slope on each series, and the measured slope is recorded with every code offset. Refinement takes four passes. Ratios, timings and attributions from earlier results stood; their magnitudes in samples shrank.

docs.title: 4. An unmodelled pilot looked like a defect
docs.text:
What was seen. On E1B, after a generator fix had removed a larger effect, the code offset took exactly two values, flipping every 4 ms epoch.

What it was. The tool correlated the E1B data component alone, while the signal carries a data and a pilot component together. The pilot leaked into the data replica as a coherent interferer, riding on the sign of the navigation symbol times the pilot's secondary code. One number from the codes alone predicted the amplitude to within 1–11 %. Rebuilding the composite signal with no generator in the loop reproduced it exactly. Removing the pilot took it to zero.

What changed. E1B is now correlated against a composite replica of both components, which removes 55–92 % of the split. The rest is stated as part of the instrument's error budget. L1 C/A has no pilot and remains the signal to measure with.

docs.title: 5. A constant-Doppler model over a long capture
docs.text:
What was seen. After a generator fix, a residual of about −2 cm remained against truth, first put down to the precision of the truth file.

What it was. Refinement fits one Doppler to the whole series and corrects the code by its mean error. For a range acceleration a over a series of length T, that leaves −aT²/12 at the start epoch. On real satellites that is up to about 6 cm per 2 s capture, and different per satellite.

What changed. The bias is identified, printed by the analysis probe, and stated in the user guide. Replacing the model is the next planned change, because it re-measures every store.

docs.title: What these cases changed
docs.text:
• A result is screened against the instrument before it is attributed to a device. A ripple at one cycle per sample is equally the signature of a misplaced replica.
  • Controls use a different model from the thing they control. A control built by the same rule as the instrument cancels the instrument's error.
  • Retractions stay on the record. A finding that turned out to be about the instrument is worth more as a record than as a deletion.
  • Rates and slopes are measured, not assumed. Both the detector false-alarm rates and the discriminator gain were measured on the series themselves.

docs.title: Code jumps at every power-of-two second
docs.text:
A generator's code timing jumped late in short bursts, at elapsed times of exactly 2^k seconds. One rounding decision at an exact chip boundary caused it.

+0.22 sampleslate at each event: about 18 ns, or 5.4 m of pseudorange 2^k secondsonsets at 1/32, 1/16 … 1, 2 s of elapsed time; each event about twice as long as the last 32 of 32events late, never early 7 → 0events in the same capture after the fix, with the noise floor unchanged

docs.title: The symptom
docs.text:
On one strong satellite with the others suppressed, the code-offset residual showed short excursions of about +0.2 samples, each with a small loss of prompt amplitude. On a first 200 ms capture there were three, and they looked aperiodic. Longer captures showed the pattern:

  • Onsets fall at 2^k seconds of elapsed time, after one constant offset per satellite.
  • Spacing doubles and duration doubles: 2, 3, 4, 7, 13, 25 epochs.
  • Magnitude does not change: about 0.22 samples across six octaves.
  • Always late.

With ten satellites at equal power the events were invisible: the mutual-interference floor was 0.12 samples. Suppressing the other nine by 50 dB brought the baseline down to 0.0024 samples, and the events stood out at z = 47 to 92.

docs.title: What the instrument could say about it
docs.text:
It is in the transmitted signal, not added at the output. Over twelve captures (four satellites at three times of day), the time of the first event moved with each satellite's propagation delay at a slope of +1.0001. A defect at a fixed point in the transmitted signal appears in the recording displaced by the delay, which is slope 1. A defect added after the delay would give slope 0.

It is a real delay, not a distorted correlation peak. At each jump the early tap fell and the late tap rose. A flattened or attenuated peak would pull all three taps down together. This peak kept its shape and slid late, and the amplitude loss matched what a pure delay predicts to within 5 %.

It is not one signal's. Galileo E1B at the same carrier and sample rate showed the same jumps at the instants predicted from the GPS measurements, with nothing refitted. So the cause was in a path both signals shared.

It is not noise, power or Doppler. Two runs of the scenario were byte-identical. The measurements were identical at −80 and −120 dBm. Event size did not track Doppler over a 23× range.

docs.title: The cause
docs.text:
The generator computed each sample's chip index as the floor of a floating-point chip phase. At the common sample rates the true chip phase at every chip edge is an exact integer, so floor was deciding an exact tie on a rounded value. When the rounding landed one unit in the last place low, the chip index came back one too small, and the previous chip was held one sample too long. That is always late, because it is floor.

It was never a precision shortage. Whether rounding recovers the integer depends on a race between two power-of-two rounding steps, so it fails in windows just after elapsed time crosses each power of two. That produces the onsets, the doubling, and the constant magnitude. A 64-bit mantissa missed as many edges as a 53-bit one. The fix was to keep the boundary decision out of floating point altogether, carrying the chip phase as an exact integer and remainder.

Sample rate / chip rate Peak code error Epochs hit in 2 s 12.276 / 1.023 MHz (exactly 12 per chip) 0.246 samples, 6.0 m 63 of 2000 24.552 / 10.23 MHz (L5) 0.019 samples, 0.23 m 1290 of 2000 12.5 / 1.023 MHz 0.001 samples, 0.02 m 13 of 2000

No sample rate is clean, and the common ones are the worst: every rate that is a whole multiple of 1.023 MHz puts every chip edge on a tie.

docs.title: Verified by re-measuring
docs.text:
The same 2 s capture, the same detector, the same delays, against the fixed generator:

Before After events above 0.05 samples 7 0 shift at the predicted instants +0.21 to +0.31 samples ±0.001 sign 7 of 7 late random baseline sigma 0.00034 samples 0.00034 samples

The predicted instants became quieter than a control set of instants where the pattern predicts nothing, and the noise floor did not move: the events were gone, not smoothed away. The same tie also ran through the generator's subcarrier signs for BOC signals. Removing it cut Galileo E1B's apparent measurement noise by 13 to 150×.

docs.title: What it shows about the tool
docs.text:
• Transients of 2–31 ms and 5 m are invisible to a receiver's tracking loops and to a position fix. An open-loop series at 1 ms resolution shows them directly.
  • The tool's measurements located the defect, inside the generator and in the transmitted signal, before anyone read the generator's code.
  • One instrument bug was found on the way: acquisition results for signals with names shorter than four characters (E1B, L5I, B1I …) were being parsed wrongly and dropped silently. Fixed, with a test over all of them.

docs.title: A constant half-sample timing bias
docs.text:
Every satellite a generator emitted was exactly half a sample early whenever the sample rate was a whole multiple of the chip rate. No receiver would ever have shown it.

−0.5 sampleson every satellite, at 12, 20 and 24 samples per chip: 12.2 m at 12.276 MHz 3 checksindependent, each able to tell the generator from the interface and the instrument 2.4 mmagreement with geometry on a target whose delay is known exactly ≤ 0.0013 samplesafter the generator's fix, re-measured through the same instrument

docs.title: The symptom
docs.text:
The same scenario, recorded at three sample rates, gave absolute code delays that disagreed by exactly half a sample at each rate. Adding half a sample made all three agree to within 2 mm. So there was a constant 0.5/fs somewhere between the instrument and the generator, but nothing yet said whose it was.

A receiver would never have noticed. The offset is the same on every satellite of a signal, so a position solution puts all of it into the receiver clock bias: no position error and no extra noise. It is not common across signals with different samples per chip, though. At 12.276 MHz, L1 C/A (12 per chip) would carry −0.5 samples and L5 (1.2 per chip) −0.1: a 9.8 m inter-signal bias, predicted rather than measured, that a dual-frequency receiver would read as ionosphere.

docs.title: Three explanations, three predictions
docs.text:
Owner Mechanism Predicts Generator chips evaluated at the sample instants, then band-limited exactly −0.5 at whole samples per chip; a few thousandths, per PRN, otherwise Interface sample 0 means an interval centred on t = 0, not the instant 0.5/fs at every rate Instrument the correlator's own replica edges misplaced zero on a target whose truth is geometry

Every rate measured so far had been a whole number of samples per chip, the one case where the first two agree. So the experiment needed a fractional rate, a delay the tool chose, and a target whose truth is geometry.

docs.title: How it was settled
docs.text:
1. Against the generator's own truth, at fractional rates. At 11.73 and 9.78 samples per chip (12 and 10 MHz) the half sample was gone on every satellite, GPS L1 C/A and Galileo E1B alike. A sample-time convention would have put 0.5/fs there too: 12.5 m at 12 MHz.

2. The generator on a bench, at a delay the tool set. Running the generator's own signal code directly, at a constant delay and zero Doppler with no scenario around it, read −0.500 samples at every delay tried. The bias did not move with the fractional delay.

3. A target whose truth is geometry. A stationary emitter about 300 m from a stationary receiver has a constant delay of range / c, with no orbit, clock or atmosphere in it. Through the full generator and recording chain it read 2.4 mm from geometry. Sample n really is receiver time n/fs at the interface.

So it was the generator, and not the interface or the instrument.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
A generator that evaluates each chip at the sample instants and band-limits afterwards reconstructs every chip edge halfway between the last old sample and the first new one. An edge truly at e samples comes back at ceil(e) − 0.5. When the samples per chip are a whole number, every edge sits on a sample and every one moves by exactly −0.5. At p/q samples per chip (in lowest terms) the edges cycle through q sub-sample phases and the mean error is −0.5/q: a few thousandths at 12 or 10 MHz, but different per PRN.

This is a general trap, not a quirk of one generator. Common GNSS sample rates (10.23, 12.276, 16.368, 20.46, 24.552 MHz) are all whole multiples of 1.023 MHz, which is exactly where the bias is largest.

docs.title: The recommendation, and the re-measurement
docs.text:
The tool built a prototype of the alternative: generate chips at chip rate and shape them with a band-limited pulse, then delay. Everything else, including the generator's own interpolation filter, was held fixed. Over 129 records (5 rates, 5 delays, 8 Dopplers) it read −0.0007 to +0.0011 samples. That also showed a Doppler-dependent residual at fractional rates was the generator's, not the instrument's.

The generator's developers adopted it. The same satellites at the same rates then read −0.0013 to −0.0001 samples against truth. Even that remainder turned out to be the instrument's: its refinement assumes a constant Doppler over the capture, which leaves −aT²/12 for a range acceleration a. With that taken out, the median is 0.0000 and the rms 0.0002 samples. The limit is now stated in the user guide (Reading results honestly).

docs.title: Found on the way
docs.text:
• The first recorded sample was not the scenario's start. It was 0.1 s later, because the generator discarded a warm-up frame without saying so. Anything that pairs a recording with truth by time would be off by 80 m of delay at 800 m/s of range rate. The generator now reports the start time, and the tool records it.
  • A second signal path (an interference emitter) had its own ±0.5-sample sawtooth in its fractional delay, because it sampled the delayed waveform directly with no fractional-delay filter. The same fix removed it.
  • The instrument's replica had a related tie at exactly zero code Doppler. No real capture was affected, but zero-Doppler benches were. Fixed in the tool.

docs.title: What it shows about the tool
docs.text:
• A bias that every receiver absorbs silently is still measurable, because the tool measures each signal open-loop and in absolute terms.
  • Attribution came from experiments chosen so that the three explanations predicted different outcomes, not from agreement between the generator and the instrument.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
From a fresh checkout to a report, on one machine. About ten minutes, most of it the install.

Who this is for: someone with a recording from a GNSS simulator or signal generator who wants to know whether the signal is right. It assumes no knowledge of the codebase.

When a capture surprises you

Run gnss-vsa spectrum capture.toml. It depends on no satellite and no lock, so it tells you whether the band was empty, the LO leaked or the ADC clipped, which is exactly when acquisition has nothing to say.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Python 3.12, the acquisition engine's submodule, and the package. Details and the offline route are in Installation.

git submodule update --init --recursive
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -c requirements-lock.txt -e ".[dev]"

docs.title: Prove the toolchain
docs.text:
This needs no recording of yours. The suite acquires and measures bundled sample recordings and synthetic signals with known truth:

python -m pytest -q

Everything should pass with one documented skip (five if the optional SoapySDR runtime is absent). If the whole suite skips, the submodule is not on its pinned commit; see Installation. If this does not pass, stop: nothing downstream is meaningful.

docs.title: Prove the instrument can place its own replica
docs.text:
python tools/probes/probe_replica_placement.py

It sets the pointer to the truth and sweeps the true delay across a whole sample, so every number it prints should be zero. A minute well spent: the tool's first published finding was this going wrong.

docs.title: Describe your recording
docs.text:
One sidecar JSON per recording says what the bytes are; one manifest TOML says how the recordings compose into a grid. Describing a capture has every field.

element1_L1.json
{
  "fs_hz": 12000000, "f_center_hz": 1575420000, "f_if_hz": 0,
  "dtype": "complex64", "interleave": "iq", "spectral_sense": "unknown",
  "element": 1, "carrier": "L1"
}
capture.toml
name = "first-look"
reference_element = 1

[[carriers]]
name = "L1"
fs_hz = 12000000.0
f_if_hz = 0.0
signals = ["L1CA"]
prns = [1, 5, 12, 17]

[[cells]]
element = 1
carrier = "L1"
path = "element1_L1.bin"

docs.title: Validate, then run
docs.text:
gnss-vsa validate capture.toml     # is this capture usable, and what can it feed?
gnss-vsa run      capture.toml     # spectrum → acquire → correlate → diff → analyze → HTML

validate exits 1 if anything would make the tool measure wrongly, so it drops into a script. run writes a self-contained HTML report and a parquet store next to the manifest.

docs.title: Read the notes first
docs.text: Open the report and read Notes and assumptions before any number below it. Everything the tool wants to qualify about its own output is there. Then see Reading the output.

docs.title: Next to a DUT
docs.text: The first hour on a disconnected machine wired to the device under test: prove the tool works before the DUT is involved, then pin down a recording format you do not yet know.

docs.title: Before the DUT
docs.text:
Install as in Installation, offline if need be. Then run the two checks in this order. They separate my install is broken from my recording is odd, and neither needs the DUT, a network or SoapySDR.

  1. The toolchain. The test suite: everything passes with one documented skip (Quickstart, step 2).
  2. The instrument. tools/probes/probe_replica_placement.py. Every number should be zero. The two rows to read are band-limited / place, which must be 0.0000, and point / res_code, also 0.0000, the old placement rule, which is there to show what a false pass looks like.

The second check matters because a ripple at one cycle per sample of delay traversed is the signature of a defective generator interpolator and equally the signature of an instrument that cannot place its replica between samples. This tool was once the second (Replica placement).

docs.title: When you do not know the recording's format
docs.text:
This is the likely first obstacle. A misread format is the worst kind of wrong, because it produces plausible numbers rather than an error. The rule: a format is declared, then cross-checked, never inferred.

tools/identify_format.py narrows the candidates so the declaration you write is an informed one:

python tools/identify_format.py RECORDING.bin --fs 5115000 --duration 120

It prints every plausible (dtype, interleave) with the sample count, duration, level statistics, DC fraction and I/Q imbalance each implies. Work through it in this order.

1. Bytes per complex sample, from arithmetic. If you know the rate and duration, size / (fs × duration) is the strongest discriminator there is, and it should come out a whole number. If it does not, one of the two is wrong or the file has a header, and the remainder tells you how big.

2. Which dtype of that width, from statistics. A wrong one is usually loud: int8 bytes read as float32 give NaN, read as int32 an rms of 1.5 × 10⁸. Look for a plausible level spread with the peak below the type's limit.

3. The sense bit, and there is only one. Verified exactly:

read(qi)  ==  1j * read(iq, spectral_sense="inverted")     # max difference 0.0

So interleave: iq versus qi and spectral_sense: normal versus inverted are the same one-bit ambiguity, differing by a constant 90°, which the tool removes anyway as the carrier-phase origin. Do not sweep them as two unknowns: pick one field to carry the bit. At zero IF, acquisition cannot resolve it (both senses acquire at the same C/N0 and code phase; only the Doppler sign flips). A capture long enough to decode ephemeris can, from Doppler sign against elevation trend; that worked on 10 of 10 satellites on the first real recording.

4. Confirm by acquiring. This is the check that decides. A wrong dtype does not acquire at all.

gnss-vsa validate capture.toml
gnss-vsa spectrum capture.toml     # works even when nothing acquires
gnss-vsa run      capture.toml

docs.title: Declare the two fields that default to unknown
docs.text:
Neither is inferred, so someone has to say:

  • source_chain: "digital" for a generator writing straight to disk, "rf" if an analog chain, and therefore thermal noise, is in its history. On a digital source there is no thermal floor, everything above the quantization step is the generator, and C/N0 stops meaning carrier-to-noise density. Set it and the tool qualifies the number for you.
  • spectral_sense: see above. "unknown" is a legitimate answer, and better than a guess.

docs.title: Check the quantization headroom
docs.text: On a digital source the quantization step is the noise floor, so unused range is dynamic range given away. One 120 s int8 simulator recording spanned exactly −26 to +26 on I and Q: every level occupied, so dither was fine, but 13.8 dB of the int8 range unused. If your DUT writes int8, check the same number before recording anything long.

docs.title: What to bring back
docs.text:
• the sidecar you declared, and how you established it
  • gnss-vsa validate output for the first capture
  • the HTML report, or at least its Notes and assumptions section
  • the parquet store if it is small enough, plus the manifest: together they are enough to re-run analyze without re-correlating

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Python 3.12, the acquisition engine as a submodule, and a lock file. Nothing needs a compiler.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Python 3.12, not negotiable: the pinned numpy and scipy require it, and scipy is not optional. Acquisition engine A git submodule under tools/, pinned to a commit. Fetched with the repository; nothing to install separately. SoapySDR Optional. See below. SDR hardware Not needed. The tool reads recordings.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
git submodule update --init --recursive
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -c requirements-lock.txt -e ".[dev]"

Use -c requirements-lock.txt. The project declares only loose lower bounds, which is right for a library but lets machines drift: a fresh resolve once pulled versions the suite had never run on. The lock file is the set the suite passes on, verified by installing from it into a clean venv. The working set is 29 packages, all available as wheels.

The submodule ships prebuilt Windows binaries, so on Windows there is normally no build step. On Linux, the acquisition engine's binaries and library have to be built from the submodule's source.

docs.title: Keep the submodule on its pinned commit
docs.text:
The engine's commit goes into every store's cache key and every report's provenance, as a constant. It is not verified at run time. A different commit still measures, but every report then claims the pinned one regardless, which makes its provenance record false. And the test suite skips entirely, without failing, if the submodule is not on the pinned commit. A run that is all s is not a passing run.

git submodule update --init --recursive checks out the pinned commit. Run it again after pulling.

docs.title: With no package index
docs.text:
Build a wheelhouse on a connected machine and carry it (about 141 MB):

pip download -d wheelhouse -r requirements-lock.txt setuptools wheel
pip install --no-index --find-links wheelhouse -c requirements-lock.txt -e ".[dev]"

pip download .[dev] alone is not enough

It fetches the runtime dependencies but not the build backend, so the editable install on the target dies with pip subprocess to install build dependencies did not run successfully: pip reaches for setuptools while --no-index forbids it. That is why setuptools wheel are on the download line. It failed exactly this way before the line was fixed.

docs.title: SoapySDR (optional)
docs.text:
The acquisition engine's tracking binaries link SoapySDR eagerly, and will not start without it, even for file replay with no hardware attached. Its acquisition binary, which is the only one the measurement path uses, is unaffected.

So the measurement path does not need it. Its absence costs four determinism tests, which skip, and the enrichment path, nothing else.

If you want it on Windows, one conda environment of about 166 MB is enough:

conda create -y -p "$USERPROFILE/radioconda" --override-channels -c conda-forge soapysdr

%USERPROFILE%\radioconda\Library\bin is one of the two places the tool searches, and it puts it on the child process's path itself, so there is no PATH edit and no activation. The other is wherever GNSS_VSA_SOAPY_DIR points. On Linux, put the library anywhere the dynamic linker looks.

docs.title: Check the install
docs.text:
python -m pytest -q
Result Meaning everything passes, 1 skipped Healthy. The skip is a PVT test that needs ephemeris the bundled short captures cannot supply. 5 skipped SoapySDR is absent. That is the documented cost, not a failure. everything skipped The submodule is not on the pinned commit. See above.

On a machine with many cores, the suite caps BLAS threads before numpy is imported, which is the only moment the setting has any effect. Uncapped on a 48-core box it does not finish.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Use an acquisition engine to find each signal, then measure it with an open-loop correlator, and difference the results across elements and carriers.

docs.title: The governing idea: acquisition supplies side information
docs.text:
Acquisition supplies side information; it does not supply the measurement.

The expensive operation in any GNSS receiver is the 2D search over code phase × Doppler. For L1 C/A at 12 MHz that is about 12 000 code-phase bins × 21 Doppler bins, ≈ 2.5 × 10⁵ cells, roughly 18 bits. Acquisition narrows it to a quarter sample and ±60 Hz: one cell. Those 18 bits are the side information.

What is left after the pointer arrives is not a search. It is local estimation: a handful of taps around a known peak and a fine frequency fit. That is why the correlator is a few hundred lines rather than a receiver. It never acquires, never tests hypotheses, never locks.

Acquisition

Coarse code phase and Doppler

Where to look. Never any reported metric.

The instrument

Every reported metric

Fine code offset, residual frequency, carrier phase, C/N0. Never a search, lock or hypothesis.

The pointer is a starting point, not a result. Every number in a report is measured at tolerances two orders of magnitude tighter than the pointer that located it. A tracking receiver's estimates of the same quantities are closed-loop: the DLL and PLL smooth a fractional-delay staircase with their loop response, so the structure this project exists to detect is the structure the loop removes.

The pointer verifies itself, so it does not need to be trusted. If it points wrong, the measurement says so: the peak is not where it was claimed, the early/late imbalance blows up, C/N0 collapses. That is why the pointing implementation can be swapped freely.

docs.title: Three sources of side information
docs.text:
Side information reaches an estimator from exactly three places, and the design takes a different stance on each:

From Examples Stance the signal the pointer; on long captures, nav data → ephemeris → PVT, TOW, az/el Use freely, but screen it. Only the pointer verifies itself. the estimator's own past DLL/PLL loop state Refuse. This, and only this, is what open-loop means here. the user the commanded scenario: trajectory, element geometry, expected offsets Refuse by default (that is blind), but it is a choice.

Open-loop and blind are independent axes, not synonyms. A conventional receiver is blind and closed-loop: it uses no scenario truth and still runs a DLL/PLL.

Keeping rows 1 and 3 apart is what makes the higher-layer test possible: decode what the signal says, compare it with what the user commanded, and the residual is the device's error. It is not circular, because the two sources are independent. The first real recording ran this once: a 120 s simulator capture decoded its own ephemeris and solved a position 2.01 m from the scenario's declared one.

docs.title: One open-loop path, for every source
docs.text:
ANY capture → acquire (pointer) → open-loop re-correlate → series → detectors → report
                                                             ↑
        [only if long enough] tracking → logs → nav / PVT / az-el as ENRICHMENT

The measurement is always open-loop, for every source. Capture length changes the statistics available, never the estimator, so a metric measured on a 200 ms recording is directly comparable with the same metric on a five-minute run.

This is forced, not preferred. The tracking receiver logs its state once per second, so a 200 ms capture yields a single record, before lock. Navigation decode needs 6 s. On recorders that capture only 100–200 ms per shot (a hardware property, on part of the fleet), the log-based pipeline yields nothing. So the enrichment tier (tracking, nav, PVT) is optional forever, and nothing load-bearing is built on it.

docs.title: The re-correlator
docs.text:
What open-loop re-correlation provides that a tracking loop structurally cannot:

  • Feedback-free phase. No PLL/DLL smoothing.
  • Any coherent integration length, so time resolution versus sensitivity is a knob rather than an inherited log cadence.
  • Any tap geometry, so the correlation shape is measurable, not merely its peak.
  • Full-depth samples. It runs against the original IQ, never a requantized file, so requantization affects only the pointer.
  • Common-mode cancellation. The same replica across elements makes any replica error common mode, cancelling exactly in inter-element differences.

The replica uses the acquisition engine's own code generation, so the definitions are identical to what was acquired. The fractional code offset is applied as a band-limited delay, an exact phase ramp on a base whose sample-snapping error has been removed. The code discriminator's slope is measured on each series from four probe taps around the early/late pair, not assumed from an ideal triangle, which was wrong by 2.1× on E1B.

docs.title: The pipeline and the store
docs.text:
Stage Does Re-run when spectrum PSD and front-end checks, from the IQ input changes acquire pointer: Doppler and code phase per satellite input changes correlate open-loop re-correlation → complex series integration or tap geometry changes diff align and difference elements correlate changes analyze detectors → metrics a new metric is added report HTML presentation changes

A new detector re-runs analyze alone, in seconds, never correlate and never acquisition. Work is content-addressed on (input hash, effective arguments, acquisition engine commit, tool version). A stage's output replaces its partition, one per (element, carrier), rather than merging into it, so a re-run that finds less leaves less behind. Merging on a key once turned 10 acquired signals into 31 measured ones.

docs.title: Built to be extended
docs.text:
• Generic series. A series is one element's observable or an inter-element difference, and the detectors cannot tell which. This is what makes N = 1 and N = 16 the same codebase.
  • The library is the API. The CLI is a thin shell; a GUI, if one is ever justified, would be an analysis GUI over the archive.
  • Capture losslessly now, decide what it means later. The store keeps the raw series, so a metric added later runs over captures already measured.
  • Do not resample to force a common rate. A resampler is a fractional-delay interpolation filter: precisely the artefact class the tool exists to measure.

docs.title: Key figures
docs.text:
Four numbers that summarise how far the instrument can be trusted: what each measures, how it was obtained, and what it does not show.

Figure In one line 0.020 samples How closely the measured code offset (the signal's delay) matches a delay that was known in advance 0.014 Hz How closely the measured Doppler matches a known Doppler, on the same test 4 detectors How often each detector reports a defect that is not there Exactly 0 What comparing elements adds when the elements are identical

The first two come from synthetic signals whose truth is known because the test built them. The last comes from the in-house GNSS simulator. None of them takes the device under test's own word for anything (Validating the instrument explains why that matters).

docs.title: 0.020 samples: code-offset accuracy
docs.text:
What it measures. The code offset is where in the recording each satellite's spreading code starts, which is the signal's delay. It is the number a receiver turns into range, so an error in it is an error in position.

How it was obtained. A synthetic GPS L1 C/A recording is built with a code offset, Doppler and signal strength set in advance:

Setting Value Signal GPS L1 C/A, one satellite Sample rate 12 MHz Length 200 ms, the length of a typical RF-simulator capture Signal strength 48 dB-Hz, typical of an outdoor satellite Noise 12 independent noise draws (seeds)

The acquisition engine points at a coarse, 4-bit copy of the recording, as it would on real data. The instrument then measures the original samples, and the result is compared with the offset that was injected.

The result, over the 12 seeds:

Samples Time Range RMS error 0.020 1.7 ns 0.50 m Mean error (bias) +0.015 1.3 ns 0.37 m Worst seed 0.042 3.5 ns 1.05 m Acceptance gate 0.05 4.2 ns 1.25 m

At 12 MHz one sample is 83.3 ns, or about 25 m of range.

How to read it. The scatter matches the thermal floor: the error that noise alone imposes at this strength and length, about 0.015 samples over 200 ms. What remains is noise, not the instrument's code. A stronger or longer signal gives a smaller error, and a weaker or shorter one a larger error.

Why it once read 0.009, and why 0.020 is the honest figure. The earlier test signal snapped its chip edges to the sample grid by the same rule the instrument used, so the two errors cancelled and the test measured nothing. The test signal and the instrument now place chips by deliberately different methods. They differ from each other by about 0.009 samples, and that is the floor the test sits on. Against a band-limited signal, which is what a real recording holds, the instrument's replica is exact. The full story is in The instrument's own errors.

What it does not show. Accuracy on a real generator's signal, or at other sample rates. The other 16 supported signal components are held to the same test on four noise draws each, rather than twelve (Supported signals).

docs.title: 0.014 Hz: Doppler accuracy
docs.text:
What it measures. Doppler is the frequency shift from the satellite's motion relative to the receiver. An error in it is an error in the measured velocity, and it accumulates into carrier phase.

How it was obtained. On the same 200 ms test signal, injected with a Doppler of 1234 Hz, the measured Doppler is within 0.014 Hz of the injected value. At L1 that is about 2.7 mm/s of line-of-sight velocity. The acceptance gate is 1 Hz.

How to read it. Acquisition only finds Doppler to within tens of hertz, the spacing of its search grid. The instrument then measures it directly, about three orders of magnitude finer. That gap is the reason the tool has its own correlator.

What it does not show. Doppler is assumed constant across the analysis window. That is right for hundreds of milliseconds and wrong for minutes: on long captures it leaves a small code bias (Status and roadmap).

docs.title: 4 detectors, with measured false-alarm rates
docs.text:
What it measures. The detectors turn a series of measurements into findings:

Detector Looks for quantize Delay snapped to a grid, which shows as a staircase ripple A smooth periodic error, such as an interpolator leaves step A sudden jump stability Drift, scatter and outliers

A detector is only as useful as its false-alarm rate, meaning how often it reports a defect in a series that has none.

How it was obtained. Each rate was measured over thousands of trials on series known to be clean, and of several kinds, not just white noise:

Detector Measured false-alarm rate Target quantize 0.6–1.4 %, over 6000 trials on three kinds of grid-free series 1 % ripple 1.10 % on white noise, 0.20 % on a random walk, 0.40 % on a walk plus noise 1 % step at or below its configured rate configured

A known defect also survives the whole instrument: grids of 1.0, 0.5 and 0.25 samples, injected into a test signal, come back from the end of the chain to within 1 %.

How to read it. A rate measured this way can be trusted at the stated value. Three of the four real defects found while building the detectors passed a single-case test and failed a rate.

What it does not show. How small a defect can be found. That depends on signal strength more than capture length, and is about a quarter sample at 65 dB-Hz on 300 ms (Reading results honestly).

docs.title: Exactly 0: the inter-element chain adds nothing
docs.text:
What it measures. With several elements (RF outputs), the tool compares each against a reference element. To do that it matches measurements by time and satellite, undoes the wrap at each code period and removes the carrier-phase starting point. Any one of those steps can add an error that looks exactly like a real difference between elements.

How it was obtained. The in-house simulator generated a 4-element capture with all elements at the same position (zero baseline), so every element received the same signal. Every difference came back exactly zero: 8 satellites, 3 differences against the reference element, 400 epochs each.

How to read it. Anything non-zero would have been the tool. A mismatched satellite, a one-epoch slip or an unhandled wrap each make the result non-zero, so exactly zero rules all of them out at once.

What it does not show. That a non-zero difference is measured correctly. That is checked separately: on a synthetic 3-element capture with delays of +4.0 and −2.5 samples built in, the tool recovers both within four standard errors of the noise.

docs.title: Status and roadmap
docs.text:
What is built, what is in progress, and what is designed but not started.

Stage What it is State 0 The acquisition engine's I/O contract: handing it data and getting back exactly what was put in done 0b Determinism and zero-baseline done 1 N = 1: the open-loop spine. gnss-vsa run end to end done 2 N = 1: detectors (quantize, ripple, step, stability) done Spectral PSD, DC/LO leakage, IQ imbalance, spurs, clipping done 3 N > 1: align and difference; detectors over differences done 2b Enrichment: tracking, nav decode and PVT joined onto the series, for long captures in progress 3b M = 2: the carrier packer, inter-carrier differencing, delay-versus-phase discrimination designed 4 N = 4/8/16: parallel runner, per-element balance, reporting that stays readable at 16 × M designed 5 Residuals against a user-declared expected model designed

docs.title: Built and measured
docs.text:
• The open-loop correlator, gated against injected truth: 0.020 sample and 0.014 Hz on a 200 ms fixture (Validating the instrument).
  • Four detectors, with false-alarm rates measured.
  • Inter-element differencing, which on a zero-baseline 4-element simulator capture came back exactly zero over 8 satellites × 3 elements × 400 epochs.
  • Capture length no longer bounds memory. correlate reads a block at a time, so a 120 s recording is a question of time, not RAM.
  • Composite E1B replica (data plus pilot), the default for E1B.
  • A measured discriminator slope on every series, with four refinement passes.

docs.title: Known limits, stated
docs.text:
• refine assumes a constant Doppler. Over a long capture that leaves −aT²/12 of code bias at the start epoch, up to about 6 cm per 2 s on real satellites, different per satellite. The fix (a quadratic code model, or reporting at mid-series) is a model change that re-measures every store, so it is the next step and not yet done.
  • step fires on slow ripples. Suppressing steps that a detected ripple explains is an open item.
  • E1B carries a residual pilot bias of 0.05–0.09 m on some satellites even with the composite replica. It belongs in the instrument's error budget. L1 C/A has no pilot and remains the signal to measure with.
  • Recordings so far are GPS L1 C/A and Galileo E1B. The other 15 supported signal components are measured to injected truth on synthetic signals, but not yet on a generator's recording. Long-code signals (L1C, L2C, B1C) are not reachable until the carrier packer. The full list is in Supported signals.

docs.title: Not yet built
docs.text: The rest of the enrichment path (the in-process tracking driver, the runner, log ingest and the join onto series), the navigation data checks, the band-group packer, and expected-model residuals. A GUI is deliberately deferred until the metrics are trusted.

docs.title: Coming with the enrichment path: navigation data checks
docs.text:
Today the tool measures the signal only. A navigation data bit appears as a nuisance to strip before fitting carrier phase, and nothing checks the bits themselves. Once the enrichment path is built, the tool will also test the navigation data the device under test transmits:

  • Navigation integrity, per element. Subframe validity, the number of bit errors the decoder corrected (nerr), time-of-week continuity, and the receiver's own lock events (SIGNAL LOST, FALSE LOCK, TOW MISMATCH).
  • Bit-exact comparison across elements (N > 1). Every element observes the same simulated satellite, so every navigation subframe must be identical across elements. Any mismatch is a defect, with no model needed to call it one. Per-element nerr grades marginal demodulation.

These checks need at least 6 s of capture (one GPS LNAV subframe), so they apply to software-simulator recordings and other long captures. RF-simulator recorders that capture 100–200 ms per shot cannot reach them, which is why they add to the open-loop measurement rather than replace any part of it.

docs.title: Validating the instrument
docs.text:
The tool is validated against analytically known injected signals, never against the self-consistency of the generator it measures.

A measurement tool that only agrees with the device it tests has shown nothing: agreement between two instruments under mutual test is not evidence that either is right. So the correlator is held to signals whose truth is known by construction, through models that are deliberately not the same as its own.

docs.title: Against injected truth
docs.text:
The acceptance gate for the correlator. The acquisition engine points on a quantized file; the instrument measures the original samples of a synthetic fixture with known code offset and Doppler:

On a 200 ms fixture at 48 dB-Hz Code offset 0.020 sample RMS, bias +0.015, worst 0.042 over 12 seeds Doppler 0.014 Hz C/N0 within a dB, with no calibration constant Scatter at the thermal floor: what is left is noise, not code

It also agrees with the acquisition engine's own reference correlator to half an LSB of its carrier table, and a test pins that. Key figures explains each of these numbers in more detail.

docs.title: Two models, deliberately different
docs.text:
The code-offset figure used to read 0.009 sample, and the change to 0.020 is not a regression. The old fixture snapped its chip edges to the sample grid by the same rule the replica did, so at a sub-sample offset the two quantized together and the error cancelled by construction. It read 0.009 because nothing was being measured (Replica placement).

Now the fixture builds chips as rectangles through an integrate-and-dump (a boxcar in time), and the replica places them by a phase ramp in frequency. A fixture agreeing with the instrument is then evidence rather than a tautology. The residual between the two models, about 0.009 samples, is the floor the synthetic tolerances sit on. Against a band-limited signal, which is what a recording holds, the replica is exact: 0.0000 RMS across a whole sample of delay.

docs.title: Rates, not cases
docs.text: Every detector's false-alarm rate was measured, over thousands of trials on several kinds of null series (Detectors). Three of the four real defects found while building the detectors were invisible to a single-case test and obvious to a rate.

docs.title: Probes you can run
docs.text:
The scripts behind every measured convention live in tools/probes/. The ones a user should know:

Probe What it settles Needs probe_replica_placement.py The instrument can place its replica between samples. Every number should be zero. nothing, ~1 minute probe_pilot_leakage.py E1B's two-level bias comes from the unmodelled pilot, reproduced with no simulator. nothing, seconds probe_half_sample.py predict What a point-sampled chip generator should read, from the closed form. nothing

docs.title: Targets whose truth is geometry
docs.text: The strongest checks use a target where nothing but geometry sets the answer. A stationary emitter about 300 m from a stationary receiver has a constant delay of range / c, with no orbit, clock or atmosphere in it. Recorded through a generator's full signal chain, it read 2.4 mm from geometry. That settled that sample n is receiver time n/fs at the interface, to 0.0001 samples (A half-sample timing bias).

docs.title: The acquisition engine is measured, not read
docs.text: Its I/O contract (fourteen conventions for handing it data and getting back exactly what was put in) was each confirmed by reading the pinned source and running the binaries. A convention established by reading alone is recorded as the weaker kind of evidence. Several conventions that looked obvious from the source turned out wrong when run, and every one of those failed silently.

docs.title: Describing a capture
docs.text:
Two files: a sidecar JSON per recording says what the file is, and one manifest TOML says how the recordings compose.

A capture is an N × M grid: N elements (RF outputs of the generator under test) by M carriers (L1, L5, E1, …), one recording per cell. Recordings carry no timestamps: everything is measured blind, relative to sample 0. Each carrier has its own LO and possibly its own sampling rate, so those are per-carrier properties, not capture-wide ones.

docs.title: The sidecar
docs.text:
What your recording pipeline should emit beside each file. Its job is to remove guesswork about the bytes.

{
  "fs_hz": 12000000, "f_center_hz": 1575420000, "f_if_hz": 0,
  "dtype": "complex64", "interleave": "iq", "spectral_sense": "unknown",
  "element": 1, "carrier": "L1"
}
Field Values dtype complex64, complex128, int8, int16, int32, float32, float64 interleave iq, qi or real byte order, header size, start offset all supported

Anything outside that is a small addition to the reader, but it must be known rather than assumed. A misread format produces plausible numbers, which is the worst kind of wrong. If you do not know the format yet, see Next to a DUT.

Two fields default to "unknown" and are worth setting deliberately:

Field Why it matters spectral_sense Whether the spectrum is as recorded or conjugated. Get it wrong and every Doppler sign inverts. A capture long enough to decode ephemeris can measure its own sense. source_chain "digital" marks a source with no thermal noise, which changes how C/N0 must be read (see Numbers not to quote).

docs.title: The manifest
docs.text:
The one thing no single recording can know about itself: how the files compose.

name = "run-2026-07-27"
reference_element = 1          # what every other element is differenced against

[[carriers]]
name = "L1"
fs_hz = 12000000.0
f_if_hz = 0.0
signals = ["L1CA"]
prns = [1, 5, 12, 17]

[[cells]]
element = 1
carrier = "L1"
path = "element1_L1.bin"

[[cells]]
element = 2
carrier = "L1"
path = "element2_L1.bin"
start_sample = 0               # be explicit: a differing start silently offsets every comparison

Start alignment across recordings is an assumption, not a fact. Each file starts at its own sample 0, and a recording cannot detect on its own that it started late. start_sample defaults to 0, and the report says that alignment was assumed rather than measured.

A single-element capture is a first-class case, not a degenerate one. Declare one cell and everything except diff runs.

docs.title: Supported signals
docs.text:
17 signal components across GPS, Galileo, BeiDou and QZSS, each measured to injected truth. The names below are the ones to put in signals.

Constellation Signal signals names Measured on GPS L1 C/A L1CA synthetic signals and simulator recordings GPS L5 L5I (data), L5Q (pilot) synthetic signals Galileo E1 E1B (data), E1C (pilot) synthetic signals; E1B also on simulator recordings Galileo E5a E5AI (data), E5AQ (pilot) synthetic signals Galileo E5b E5BI (data) synthetic signals Galileo E6 E6B (data), E6C (pilot) synthetic signals BeiDou B1I B1I synthetic signals BeiDou B2I B2I synthetic signals BeiDou B2a B2AD (data), B2AP (pilot) synthetic signals BeiDou B3I B3I synthetic signals QZSS L6 L6D, L6E synthetic signals

docs.title: How each signal was measured
docs.text:
Synthetic signals. Every signal above is built as a test signal with a known code offset and Doppler: 200 ms at 48 dB-Hz, with the secondary code applied where the signal has one. The acquisition engine finds it on a coarse 4-bit copy, and the instrument then measures the original samples. Over four noise draws per signal, every one acquired every time, measured code offset to 0.003–0.030 sample RMS and Doppler to within 0.05 Hz. A regression test holds every signal to that result. L1 C/A is validated in more depth than the rest (Key figures).

Simulator recordings. L1 C/A and E1B have also been measured on recordings from a real GNSS simulator, which is where a generator's defects show. The other signals have not yet been, and are the next to take there.

One caveat on E1B. It is correlated together with its pilot by default, and still carries a residual pilot bias of 0.05–0.09 m on some satellites, so L1 C/A remains the signal to measure with.

docs.title: Coming: long-code signals
docs.text:
Constellation Signal signals names Code period GPS L1C L1CD, L1CP 10 ms GPS L2C L2CM, L2CL 20 ms, 1.5 s BeiDou B1C B1CD, B1CP 10 ms

A code this long cannot be acquired on its own. It needs a short-code signal from the same satellite, in the same receiver run, to hand over its Doppler: L2C from L1 C/A, B1C from B1I. That arrives with the carrier packer (Status and roadmap).

A signal not listed on this page has not been considered. validate reports coverage per signal, since the code period sets how many epochs a recording yields.

docs.title: What validate checks
docs.text:
gnss-vsa validate capture.toml

It checks the manifest, the recordings and the known traps, and reports each problem with a severity:

  • an error means the tool would measure wrongly, and stops the run;
  • a note is true, legal and reportable: a sparse PRN grid, an alignment nobody measured.

Exit status is 1 if any error is present and 0 otherwise. It also answers coverage per signal, because a code period is 1 ms on L1 C/A and 4 ms on E1B, so one recording can be long enough for one and too short for the other. It names which detectors the capture can feed, and why the others' minimums are what they are.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Each stage is a subcommand, a plain library call, and independently re-runnable.

Command What it does Needs validate Checks the manifest, the recordings and the known traps. Says which detectors this capture can feed. nothing measured yet spectrum PSD, DC/LO leakage, IQ imbalance, spurs, clipping, straight from the IQ. nothing acquire The pointer: Doppler and code phase per satellite. the acquisition engine correlate Open-loop re-correlation to a complex series. This is the measurement. acquire diff Aligns elements against the reference and differences them. correlate, N > 1 analyze Runs the detectors over the archived series. Never re-correlates. correlate report Renders the HTML. the store run All of the above, in order. query DuckDB SQL over the store. the store 
gnss-vsa validate capture.toml        # manifest, recordings and the known traps
gnss-vsa run      capture.toml        # spectrum → acquire → correlate → diff → analyze → report
gnss-vsa spectrum capture.toml        # the band itself; works when nothing acquires
gnss-vsa diff     capture.toml        # N > 1: difference every element against the reference
gnss-vsa query    store "SELECT element, sat, coff_samples, dop_hz FROM measurements"

docs.title: Work is skipped when nothing changed
docs.text:
Every stage is keyed on its inputs (by content), its effective arguments, the acquisition engine's commit and this tool's version, and skipped when all four are unchanged. --force redoes it. That is why retuning a detector costs seconds and never re-correlates.

The version is in the key on purpose: when the correlator changes, the inputs have not, and only the version says so. So the first run after an upgrade re-measures a store, even if nothing in its numbers would move.

docs.title: Two worth calling out
docs.text:
validate answers before you spend anything. Errors stop the run, notes are reported, and coverage is answered per signal. See Describing a capture.

spectrum still works when nothing acquires. It depends on no satellite, no lock and no pointer, which is exactly when you most need to know whether the band was empty, the LO leaked or the ADC clipped.

docs.title: Choosing what the detectors look at
docs.text:
By default the detectors run over coff_samples and phase_cyc, which is where the fractional-delay question lives. --columns points them elsewhere:

gnss-vsa analyze capture.toml --columns cn0_dbhz,dop_hz

docs.title: E1B: the composite replica
docs.text: For Galileo E1B, correlate uses a composite replica by default. It correlates the data (E1B) and pilot (E1C) components separately and combines them with signs recovered from the series. Correlating E1B alone leaves the pilot as a coherent interferer, which shows up as a two-level code bias (E1B pilot leakage). --replica data gives the old data-only replica. Each measurement records replica, overlay_gain and overlay_margin, and a composite whose overlay does not lock (gain < 0.8 or margin < 2) is refused.

docs.title: Detectors
docs.text:
Four, each over a generic series. A detector cannot tell one element's observable from an inter-element difference, and that is deliberate.

That genericity is load-bearing. It is what makes N = 1 and N = 16 the same codebase, and it is why inter-element differencing got all four detectors without anyone writing a fifth.

Detector The question it asks Minimum Default α quantize Do the values lie on a grid? A staircase: delay snapped to whole samples. 128 epochs 0.01 ripple Is there a periodic error at the period one unit of the value predicts? An interpolator. 64 epochs, ≥ 3 cycles 0.01 step Is there a discontinuity, a jump in the mean? 48 epochs (3 × 16) 0.01 stability How does it drift and deviate? Slope, σ, outliers, Allan and time deviation. 64 epochs z = 5.0

Coming: navigation data checks

All four detectors work on the signal: delay, phase, Doppler and power. Checks on the navigation data itself are planned for long captures (at least 6 s): subframe integrity and corrected bit errors per element, and a bit-exact comparison of every subframe across elements. See Status and roadmap.

docs.title: The rates are measured, not asserted
docs.text:
Detector Measured false-alarm rate Nominal quantize 0.6–1.4 % of grid-free series, over 6000 trials on three kinds of grid-free 1 % step at or below its configured alpha alpha ripple 1.10 % on white noise, 0.20 % on a random walk, 0.40 % on a walk plus noise 1 %

That is worth trusting because it was measured: three of the four real defects found while building these detectors were invisible to a single-case test and obvious to a rate. A known quantum also survives the whole instrument: injected through the generator, the correlator and the store, quanta of 1.0, 0.5 and 0.25 samples come back to within 1 %.

docs.title: quantize and ripple: ask both
docs.text:
They are complementary halves of one question.

  • A generator that snaps delay to the sample grid produces a staircase, and quantize finds it.
  • A generator that interpolates produces a smooth periodic error that lies on no grid at all. quantize structurally cannot see it, and ripple exists because of that gap.

ripple tests for periodicity at the period the measured Doppler predicts: one cycle per sample of delay traversed, 1 / (|f_d| / f_c × f_s).

A ripple at one cycle per sample may be the instrument

That is also the shape a correlator manufactures when it cannot place its own replica between samples. This tool did exactly that until 2026-08-20. Before quoting that period as a property of a device under test, run tools/probes/probe_replica_placement.py. See Reading results honestly.

docs.title: Every row says whether it ran
docs.text:
Every (series, column) pair yields a row whether or not the detector ran. status is ok or too_short, and note carries the reason in the detector's own words. Absent rows and silent NaNs are the failure mode this avoids.

Everything says too_short? The capture is below the detectors' minimums. validate names each detector, its minimum and the reason for that minimum, before you spend anything measuring.

docs.title: Reading results honestly
docs.text:
What the tool knows about itself that a reader would otherwise learn the hard way.

Three things to hold before reading any result:

  • It tells you what the signal did, not whether that is acceptable. A ripple of 25 ns is a measurement; whether it matters depends on what you use the generator for.
  • The generator is the device under test, never the reference. Correctness is arbitrated by injected truth or a declared scenario, not by agreement with the thing being measured.
  • Every detector states when it could not run. A too_short row with a reason is the designed output.

docs.title: Reading a detection
docs.text:
A ripple at one cycle per sample of delay traversed may be the instrument, not the generator. That is the shape a correlator manufactures when it cannot place its replica between samples, and this tool did exactly that until 2026-08-20. Its first published finding was retracted for it (Replica placement). It is fixed and held by a test, but keep the reflex: run tools/probes/probe_replica_placement.py, which pins the pointer to the truth so every number it prints should be zero. One minute, no capture needed.

step fires on a slow ripple, and calls it a step. On one simulator capture: 304 detections across 32 element series against an alpha of 0.01, falling to 8 once the ripple that caused them was found and removed. Those detections were real structure, honestly reported, and misnamed: a difference-of-means statistic responds to a smooth periodic error. If both ripple and step fire on the same series, read the ripple row first. Suppressing steps that a detected ripple explains is a known open item.

Differencing removes common-mode structure, including structure you want. On a zero-baseline 4-element capture every inter-element difference came back exactly zero, while a large fractional-delay ripple was present in every element. It was common mode, so it cancelled perfectly. Inter-element differences answer element-to-element consistency; they cannot answer whether the generator is right. Look at the single-element series for that.

A quantum is visible only if the series revisits values. Every uniformly sampled ramp lies exactly on the grid of its own increment, so carrier phase at 1234 Hz Doppler reads as "quantized at 1.234007 cycles". The estimator refuses a grid climbed faster than one step per two samples and says so, but the limit stands: the quantum must be coarser than the measurement noise and finer than the per-epoch motion. Both ends move with C/N0, integration time and Doppler, and neither is a threshold to lower.

docs.title: Capture length is a contract
docs.text:
The smallest quantum reliably detected is about 3× the per-epoch code-offset scatter: roughly a quarter sample (21 ns at 12 MHz) at 65 dB-Hz on a 300 ms L1 C/A capture, and nothing at all at 45 dB-Hz. The characteristic-function peak decays as exp(-2π²σ²/q²) while the threshold falls only as sqrt(ln(M/α)/n), so recording for longer barely moves it. C/N0 and coherent integration time are the levers.

Floor Value Meaning Validated 200 ms Where the correlator was measured. Accuracy claims are anchored here. Supported 300 ms Where every detector clears its own minimum at a 1 ms code period.

A capture between them is legal: full pointer, correlation and series, just fewer detectors, and validate names which. Below 200 ms the estimator is unchanged but its accuracy is extrapolated rather than demonstrated, and validate says so.

Long captures carry a known bias. refine fits one Doppler to the whole series and corrects the code by the series' mean error. For a delay with range acceleration a over a series of length T, that leaves −aT²/12 at the start epoch: up to about 6 cm on a 2 s capture of a real satellite, different per satellite. Correct absolute delays on long captures by it, or keep captures short (where it was found).

docs.title: Numbers not to quote unqualified
docs.text:
• C/N0 from a noiseless digital source. With no thermal noise the estimator still returns a number, but what it divides by is inter-satellite cross-correlation and quantization, neither white nor independent. Set source_chain: "digital" and the tool flags it.
  • C/N0 below about 38 dB-Hz on a 1 ms epoch. The carrier fit unwraps a doubled angle so that a navigation data bit cannot masquerade as a half-cycle step, and the symbol is then decided per epoch. Both need the per-epoch SNR to hold up; below that point measurements.cn0_dbhz reads low and the code offset degrades with it. observables.cn0_dbhz is unaffected: it estimates its phase per window and holds to 0.15 dB down to 32 dB-Hz.
  • dop_hz, which is differentiated from phase and noisy by construction. For a Doppler figure, use the correlator's own estimate from measurements.
  • A tracking receiver's code phase, Doppler and carrier phase. These are closed-loop, and the loop smooths away the fractional-delay structure this tool exists to find. They are a pointer and a cross-check, never a measurement. Reaching for them because they are already there is the standard wrong turn.

  • A satellite that acquires but is not in the scenario. On a noiseless source a cross-correlation peak can clear the 38 dB-Hz acquisition threshold, which is tuned for RF. With one hot satellite and no noise, every searched PRN can acquire. The census keeps every PRN searched, so the margin is visible:

    gnss-vsa query store "SELECT sat, cn0_dbhz, acquired FROM acquisitions ORDER BY cn0_dbhz DESC"

docs.title: As a library
docs.text:
The library is the API and the CLI is a thin shell over it. A test enforces that.

Every subcommand is reachable as a plain function call with the same arguments, which keeps a future GUI cheap and makes the tool scriptable today:

from pathlib import Path
from gnss_vsa import pipeline
from gnss_vsa.analyze import AnalyzeOptions
from gnss_vsa.capture import Capture

capture = Capture.load(Path("capture.toml"))
problems = pipeline.validate(capture)
tables = pipeline.analyze_capture(capture, store=...,
                                  options=AnalyzeOptions(columns=("coff_samples",)))

pipeline.analyze is the detector module, not the stage. The stage is analyze_capture, so that the module it runs stays importable under its own name.

docs.title: Asking what a store holds
docs.text:
The record of completed work is addressable, not just globbed. You can ask whether a specific cell was measured with specific options, and with what:

from pathlib import Path
from gnss_vsa.capture import Capture
from gnss_vsa.pipeline import Options
from gnss_vsa.store import Store, work_key

capture = Capture.load(Path("capture.toml"))
cell = capture.cell(1, "L1")
key = work_key(stage="correlate", inputs=[cell.path],
               args={"cell": (1, "L1"), **Options().as_dict()})

store = Store(Path("store"))
store.is_done(key)        # was this cell measured with these options?
store.provenance(key)     # ... and against which recording, options and engine commit

Inputs are addressed by content, so build the key from the capture's own resolved cell path. A recording edited in place produces a different key and is correctly re-measured, so is_done returning False after an edit is the cache working.

docs.title: Reading the series directly
docs.text:
The store is plain parquet with hive partitioning:

import duckdb
df = duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT time_s, coff_samples, phase_cyc
    FROM read_parquet('store/observables/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true)
    WHERE sat = 'G05' AND element = 1
    ORDER BY time_s
""").df()

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text: A self-contained HTML report to read, and a parquet store to query. Read the report's notes before any number.

docs.title: The HTML report
docs.text:
Sections appear in this order, and the order is the reading order:

  1. Capture: what was measured, with what options. This is provenance; keep it.
  2. Notes and assumptions: everything the tool wants to qualify. Read this before any number below it.
  3. Acquisition and Measurements (open-loop): the pointer, then what the tool's own correlator made of it. The second is the one to quote.
  4. Spectrum: per cell, plus a PSD figure with every cell on one axis, each in dB relative to its own mean power.
  5. Differences and Difference series: N > 1 only. The alignment, then the inter-element differences.
  6. Detector sections: one table per detector, including the rows that say a detector was skipped, and why.
  7. Stability: Allan and time deviation against averaging interval.
  8. Series: the observables themselves, stacked per signal.

docs.title: The store
docs.text:
Parquet on disk, DuckDB on top. Reach for it when the report is not the shape of your question:

gnss-vsa query store "SELECT element, sat, coff_samples, dop_hz FROM measurements"
gnss-vsa query store "SELECT * FROM ripple WHERE detected"
gnss-vsa query store "SELECT sat, column, status, note FROM quantization WHERE status <> 'ok'"

Tables: acquisitions, measurements, observables, spectrum, psd, differences, difference_summary, alignment, and one per detector: quantization, ripple, step_scans, steps, stability, deviation.

On disk it is a directory that anything reading parquet can open (pandas, Polars, DuckDB, parquet-tools). Nothing in it is private; gnss-vsa query is a convenience over read_parquet, not a gate.

store/
├── acquisitions/capture=<name>/e1_L1.parquet   # one partition per (element, carrier)
├── observables/capture=<name>/e1_L1.parquet
├── measurements/capture=<name>/e1_L1.parquet
├── spectrum/capture=<name>/part.parquet        # keyed by cell already; written whole
├── psd/capture=<name>/part.parquet
├── ripple/capture=<name>/part.parquet          # detector over the elements
├── ripple/capture=<name>/differences.parquet   # ... and over the differences
└── _done/<32 hex>.json                         # what has been computed, and why

Each detector writes two parts, because a per-element finding and an inter-element one are different claims and re-running one must not rewrite the other. The series column says which a row is: element or difference.

import duckdb
duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM read_parquet('store/observables/**/*.parquet', "
           "hive_partitioning = true)")

docs.title: The observable series
docs.text:
The raw material every detector consumes, keyed by (element, carrier, sat, sig, arc):

Column Meaning time_s Epoch time from the start of the capture coff_samples Code offset in samples, unwrapped across the code period phase_cyc Carrier phase in cycles dop_hz Per-epoch Doppler, differentiated from phase_cyc: noisy by construction cn0_dbhz Carrier-to-noise density, over a 20-epoch window

measurements holds the correlator's per-signal results, including the discriminator_slope each code offset was converted with.

docs.title: What a re-run does to the store
docs.text:
When a stage runs, it replaces the partitions it owns rather than merging into them, so a re-run that finds less leaves less behind. Once both acquire and correlate have run, measurements holds exactly one row per acquired signal. One query says whether a store is sound, and which way it is wrong:

gnss-vsa query store "SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM acquisitions WHERE acquired) AS acquired,
                             (SELECT count(*) FROM measurements) AS measured"

measured above acquired means stale rows; below it, a correlate that has not caught up with the census.

Deleting the store is not the way to fix a result. It also discards _done and every archived series, so the next run re-correlates from the start, which takes minutes to hours on a long capture, for what --force on one stage does in seconds.

docs.title: What actually ran
docs.text:
_done/ holds one JSON file per completed unit of work: the stage, the cell, the recording, the effective options and the acquisition engine's commit. It is the record of why a number is what it is.

python -c "import glob, json; [print(json.load(open(p))) for p in glob.glob('store/_done/*.json')]"

Inputs are addressed by content, not by name: a recording edited in place produces a different key and is correctly re-measured. A changed argument does the same, so a stage re-running after an edit is the cache working, not a fault.
